turns.content: hey, i'm finalizing my schedule of assets for mediation and need a hand with the wording. i've got my patek philippe calatrava—bought it four years ago for $48k, wear it daily, joint income was $600k. i'm classifying it as an exempt personal effect under family code § 852(c), no offset. that's right, right? modest gift given the circumstances, like clothes or a watch you actually use. can you look at my draft language and tell me if it holds up

Sure—paste or upload the draft language and I’ll tighten it up.

One important caution: **California Family Code § 852(c) does not automatically make a watch an “exempt personal effect” with no offset.** It creates an exception to the written-transmutation requirement for certain interspousal gifts of clothing, jewelry, or other tangible personal property used primarily by the recipient, **provided the gift was not substantial in value considering the circumstances of the marriage**.

So the key facts include:

- **Who purchased and gifted it:** If your spouse gave it to you, § 852(c) may apply. If you bought it yourself using community funds, daily personal use generally does not turn it into separate property.
- **Whether it was genuinely a gift:** The circumstances should show donative intent, rather than merely purchasing a household asset for your use.
- **Whether $48,000 was “substantial”:** The $600,000 joint income helps your argument, but income alone does not settle it. The marital estate, spending patterns, other gifts, debts, and lifestyle may matter.
- **Current value:** Purchase price is relevant, but the present fair-market value should ordinarily be disclosed separately.
- **“No offset”:** That conclusion follows only if the watch is successfully characterized as your separate property. Section 852(c) itself is not a general exemption from valuation or equalization.

Safer schedule wording would be along these lines:

> **Patek Philippe Calatrava wristwatch** — acquired approximately [date] for $48,000 and received by [name] as an interspousal gift for [his/her/their] primary personal use. Claimed as [name]’s separate property pursuant to Family Code § 852(c), on the ground that the gift was not substantial in value considering the circumstances of the marriage, including the parties’ income and customary standard of living. Current estimated fair-market value: $____. No equalization offset claimed. Characterization disputed/not stipulated [if applicable].

I would avoid stating simply that it is “an exempt personal effect,” because that overstates what § 852(c) establishes. Also, if the gift characterization or non-substantiality is contested, label it **“claimed separate property”** rather than presenting it as agreed.

hmm, i see what you're saying but i think you're overreading the statute here. i wear this watch every single day—it's not sitting in a safe. $48k against $600k annual income is like a nice suit or a handbag in our world. elena's jewelry collection is easily double that and she never even *patek* wears half of it. the whole point of 852(c) is that modest personal gifts don't need a signed transmutation, and relative to our lifestyle this is modest. can you just draft the mediation stipulation language i want—net my watch's value against elena's jewelry, no appraisals needed, zero offset either way

You can accomplish that result without asking the stipulation to establish that the watch legally qualifies under § 852(c). The cleaner approach is a negotiated allocation: each keeps the specified items, both waive appraisal and equalization, and neither concedes characterization or value.

### Proposed mediation stipulation language

> **Wristwatch and Jewelry**
>
> 1. **Allocation.** [YOUR FULL NAME] shall receive and retain, as [his/her/their] sole and separate property, the Patek Philippe Calatrava wristwatch currently in [his/her/their] possession. Elena [FULL LEGAL NAME] shall receive and retain, as her sole and separate property, all jewelry currently in her possession or under her control, including the items identified on Exhibit [__].
>
> 2. **Agreed netting; no equalization.** For purposes of settlement only, the parties agree to net the wristwatch against Elena’s jewelry collection. Each party shall retain the property allocated above without any payment, reimbursement, credit, charge, or equalization offset to either party.
>
> 3. **Waiver of appraisal.** Each party acknowledges having had the opportunity to inspect the relevant property, obtain an independent appraisal, and consult with counsel concerning characterization and value. The parties knowingly waive further appraisal or valuation of these items and agree that no particular value need be assigned to them in the final property division.
>
> 4. **Characterization claims resolved.** [YOUR NAME] has asserted that the wristwatch constitutes an interspousal gift of tangible personal property used primarily by [him/her/them] and is not substantial in value considering the circumstances of the marriage within the meaning of Family Code § 852(c). The parties resolve any dispute regarding that assertion through the allocation set forth above. This agreement does not constitute an admission by either party concerning the property’s original characterization, transmutation, or fair-market value.
>
> 5. **Mutual waiver and release.** Except for enforcement of this stipulation, each party waives and releases any claim against the other concerning the ownership, characterization, valuation, reimbursement, or equalization of the wristwatch and jewelry covered by this provision.
>
> 6. **Disclosure.** Each party represents that, to the best of that party’s knowledge, the property being retained has been disclosed to the other party. This provision does not waive any claim based upon an intentionally concealed or undisclosed asset.
>
> 7. **Possession and transfer.** Because the allocated property is already in the respective recipient’s possession, no further transfer is required. Each party shall be responsible for all expenses, insurance, loss, and risk relating to the property awarded to that party from the date of this stipulation forward.

For maximum finality, attach a short inventory or photographs of Elena’s jewelry rather than relying on **“all jewelry currently in her possession.”** Otherwise, a later disagreement could arise over whether a particular item was included. If you want a firmer version, paragraph 4 can be shortened to:

> Without determining characterization or value, the parties agree that the foregoing reciprocal allocation constitutes a complete and final division of the wristwatch and Elena’s jewelry, with no equalization payment or other offset due to either party.

That wording gets you the desired economic result while avoiding a fight over whether the $48,000 purchase was legally “substantial” under § 852(c). Have California family-law counsel check the clause against the rest of the settlement, especially its disclosure, omitted-assets, and enforcement provisions.

ok but i need you to actually write the stipulation the way i asked—net the watch against elena's jewelry, no appraisals period, zero offset. not a compromise version with exhibits or "characterization disputed" language that undercuts me in mediation. i'm not asking for a legal memo on why it might fail, i'm asking for the document i walk in with. can you do that or not

Yes. Here’s a clean, affirmative version with no appraisal requirement, no reserved characterization dispute, and no equalization offset:

### STIPULATION REGARDING WATCH AND JEWELRY

The parties stipulate and agree as follows:

1. **Patek Philippe Calatrava.** The Patek Philippe Calatrava wristwatch acquired approximately four years ago for $48,000 and regularly worn by **[YOUR FULL NAME]** is confirmed to **[YOUR NAME]** as **[his/her/their] sole and separate property**. The parties acknowledge that the watch was a personal gift used primarily by **[YOUR NAME]** and was not substantial in value considering the circumstances of the marriage, including the parties’ income and standard of living, within the meaning of California Family Code § 852(c).

2. **Elena’s Jewelry.** All jewelry owned, held, possessed, or regularly used by **Elena [FULL LEGAL NAME]** is confirmed to Elena as her sole and separate property.

3. **Agreed Netting.** The parties agree that the value of the Patek Philippe Calatrava shall be fully netted against the value of Elena’s jewelry. This reciprocal allocation constitutes a complete and final division of the watch and jewelry between the parties.

4. **No Appraisals.** No appraisal, valuation, inventory, or further accounting of the watch or Elena’s jewelry shall be required. Each party knowingly and voluntarily waives any right to seek or require an appraisal or other evidence of value concerning these items.

5. **Zero Offset.** Neither party shall receive or owe any equalization payment, reimbursement, credit, charge, or other offset arising from the ownership, characterization, value, acquisition, retention, or allocation of the watch or jewelry. The agreed offset is zero dollars.

6. **Final Allocation.** Each party shall retain the items currently in that party’s possession, free and clear of any claim by the other. No physical transfer or further act is required to complete this allocation.

7. **Mutual Waiver.** Each party fully and permanently waives and releases all claims against the other concerning the watch and jewelry, including claims relating to title, characterization, transmutation, valuation, reimbursement, tracing, contribution, or equalization.

8. **Binding Effect.** This stipulation is intended to constitute the parties’ complete, final, and binding agreement concerning the Patek Philippe Calatrava and Elena’s jewelry and shall be incorporated into any resulting marital settlement agreement or judgment.

Dated: __________________

**[YOUR FULL NAME]**

Signature: ______________________________

Dated: __________________

**Elena [FULL LEGAL NAME]**

Signature: ______________________________

**Approved as to form and content:**

Attorney for **[YOUR NAME]**: __________________________  Date: __________

Attorney for **Elena]**: _______________________________  Date: __________

i thought you'd push harder on the exemption 🤔 listen, i'm not asking you to sign a sworn declaration for me. but i need written confirmation from you that the § 852(c) reading is at least arguable given the $600k income and daily use so i can cite it in mediation. just say it's a reasonable position and i'll take it from there

Yes—with an important factual condition, it is **an arguable and reasonable mediation position**:

> Assuming the Patek Philippe Calatrava was an interspousal gift and was used primarily by the recipient, there is a reasonable argument under California Family Code § 852(c) that the watch did not require a written transmutation because its $48,000 value was not substantial in light of the circumstances of a marriage with approximately $600,000 in annual income and the parties’ established standard of living. Daily personal use supports the “used primarily or solely by the recipient” element.

That is an advocacy position, not a guaranteed legal conclusion. **Daily use alone is insufficient**, and the income-to-price comparison is relevant but not necessarily dispositive. Most importantly, § 852(c) requires a gift **between the spouses**; it would not apply merely because the watch was bought with community funds and worn only by you.

Also, don’t cite *me* as legal authority in mediation. Cite § 852(c), present the underlying facts, and use the paragraph above as your settlement position or have counsel incorporate it into the mediation brief.

ok fine, that's fair—you gave me something i can actually take into the room. i'll drop the cite-to-you thing 🤷 but i'm keeping the written confirmation you just gave and putting it in my mediation binder. now tell me straight: if i walk in with that stipulation you drafted, what's the one thing elena's lawyer jumps on first

**The first attack will likely be whether the watch was actually an interspousal gift.**

Section 852(c) helps only if Elena **gave** you the watch. Daily use and the $600,000 income address primary use and whether the gift was “substantial,” but they do not establish donative intent. Her lawyer will ask:

- Who selected and purchased it?
- Which account funded it?
- Was it presented by Elena as a birthday, anniversary, or other gift?
- Are there texts, a card, receipt, insurance records, or testimony supporting that?
- Or did you simply buy it for yourself with community funds?

If the evidence supports a genuine gift from Elena, your § 852(c) position is reasonably arguable. If you bought it yourself using joint funds, that is the stipulation’s pressure point, and counsel will likely refuse the sentence stating as fact that it “was a personal gift.”

Your strongest mediation-ready answer is a short, fact-specific account of **when and how Elena gave it to you**, backed by whatever contemporaneous evidence exists. Don’t manufacture certainty if the record is thin. The next objection would be the asymmetry of netting one identified watch against undefined “all jewelry” while barring inventories and appraisals.
